extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and investigators of nature (readers seeking a method for scientific inquiry)
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive method for conducting natural philosophy: how to observe, reason from, and experimentally investigate nature to discover true axioms and control nature. Emphasizes procedures, epistemic safeguards, and common pitfalls in scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism and scepticism; test by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “They who have presumed to dogmatize on nature... have inflicted the greatest injury...”; contrasted with those who assert nothing can be known. The better course is not to dispute about the possibility of knowledge but to put it to the test of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not settle claims by rhetorical dogma nor give up inquiry through sceptical despair; instead, adopt experimental testing as the arbiter of claims. Prefer practical demonstration over professorial disputation; require careful, experiential proof before accepting doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from actual sensory perceptions; restore senses to their rank
rubrics_metrics.description: “It consists in determining the degrees of certainty, while we... restore the senses to their former rank, but generally reject that operation of the mind which follows close upon the senses, and open and establish a new and certain course... from the first actual perceptions of the senses themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start inquiry at the level of concrete observations. Treat sense-perceptions as the primary data and resist premature mental operations that abstract too soon. Direct the mind from first perceptions with a disciplined procedure rather than relying on unaided intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments and mechanical aids to extend the understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: “Effects are produced by the means of instruments and helps, which the understanding requires no less than the hand... If men had attempted mechanical labors with their hands alone... they would have been able to move and overcome but little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ instruments and experimental apparatus to amplify and regulate observation and experiment. Do not rely solely on unaided faculties of the mind; design and use tools to enable investigations inaccessible to bare senses or unaided thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge must seek causes; knowledge and human power are synonymous
rubrics_metrics.description: “Knowledge and human power are synonymous, since the ignorance of the cause frustrates the effect; for nature is only subdued by submission, and that which in contemplative philosophy corresponds with the cause in practical science becomes the rule.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful scientific inquiry aims to understand causes so that nature can be harnessed. Prioritize causal understanding rather than mere cataloguing of effects; a valid discovery should enable control or useful application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine induction: build axioms from particulars ascending gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our only hope, then, is in genuine induction.” “There are but two ways of investigating and discovering truth... The other constructs its axioms from the senses and particulars, by ascending continually and gradually, till it finally arrives at the most general axioms, which is the true but unattempted way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct general principles only after systematically arranging many well-chosen particulars and observations. Avoid leaping from a few instances to sweeping axioms; instead, ascend by regular and cumulative induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject syllogism/received logic as the method of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: “As the present sciences are useless for the discovery of effects, so the present system of logic is useless for the discovery of the sciences... The syllogism... forces assent, therefore, and not things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat syllogistic deduction or rhetorical logic as a means of discovering new truths; logic may confirm or force assent but cannot replace empirical induction. Use logic after discovery, not as the primary discovery engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form clear, well-defined notions; avoid vague abstract terms
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have no sound notions either in logic or physics; substance, quality, action, passion, and existence are not clear notions... much less weight, levity, density...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize and refine concepts before using them. Avoid relying on ambiguous, traditional, or fantastical terms; define terms with reference to regularized observations and experiments to prevent confusion and sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penetrate remote and hidden parts of nature beyond superficial experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is necessary... to penetrate the more secret and remote parts of nature, in order to abstract both notions and axioms from things by a more certain and guarded method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inquiry to reach less obvious phenomena and deeper orders of nature rather than only common-sense effects. Use systematic experiments targeted to reveal hidden mechanisms and subtle processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make an instauration from the foundations; avoid merely adding to old systems
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is in vain to expect any great progress in the sciences by the superinducing or ingrafting new matters upon old. An instauration must be made from the very foundations...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When methods or premises are fundamentally defective, rebuild methods from first principles rather than attempting superficial repairs. Be willing to restructure foundational approaches to inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish anticipation of the mind from interpretation of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “We call that human reasoning which we apply to nature the anticipation of nature (as being rash and premature), and that which is properly deduced from things the interpretation of nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of prematurely imposed hypotheses or a priori reasoning (anticipations). Prefer interpretations strictly grounded in systematic empirical evidence and ordered induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring men to particulars and their regular series and order
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must bring men to particulars and their regular series and order, and they must for a while renounce their notions, and begin to form an acquaintance with things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure inquiry by collecting and ordering particular instances into regular series; require temporary suspension of ingrained concepts to let particulars inform generalization. Emphasize cataloguing and ordering of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apt and fit experiments judged by the senses; experiment and the thing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the better interpretations of nature are worked out by instances, and fit and apt experiments, where the senses only judge of the experiment, the experiment of nature and the thing itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that directly test the phenomenon and let sensory-observed experimental outcomes guide inference. Prefer well-designed, relevant experiments over speculative argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four idols: identify and guard against cognitive impediments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Four species of idols beset the human mind... the Idols of the Tribe, the Den, the Market, the Theatre.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cognitive obstacles (the four idols) as explicit sources of error and apply procedural safeguards to mitigate them (see individual idols for specifics). Treat the doctrine of idols as central to avoiding sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idols of the Tribe: human nature's biases and sensory/mental limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The idols of the tribe are inherent in human nature... man’s sense is falsely asserted to be the standard of things... the human mind resembles uneven mirrors which impart their own properties to different objects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for universal human cognitive tendencies—error-prone senses, eagerness for generality, imagination, and passion. Use methods and instruments that correct or compensate for these species-wide distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idols of the Den: individual biases from temperament, education, and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: “The idols of the den are those of each individual... from his own peculiar and singular disposition, or from his education and intercourse with others, or from his reading... the spirit of man is variable, confused, and as it were actuated by chance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-critical about personal preconceptions and disciplinary blind spots. Encourage diversity of approaches and cross-checks to counteract individual preoccupations and entrenched habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idols of the Market: errors arising from language and social communication
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are also idols formed by the reciprocal intercourse and society of man with man, which we call idols of the market... words are formed at the will of the generality, and there arises from a bad and unapt formation of words a wonderful obstruction to the mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about how words and common language shape thought; avoid being misled by popular usages or ambiguous terms. Resolve disputes by careful definition but ultimately rely on ordered instances rather than verbal wrangling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idols of the Theatre: errors from accepted philosophical systems and false demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Idols which have crept into men’s minds from the various dogmas of peculiar systems of philosophy... we regard all the systems of philosophy hitherto received or imagined, as so many plays brought out and performed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat entrenched theoretical systems skeptically when they are detached from empirical verification. Do not accept elaborate systems merely because they are fashionable or rhetorically satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative instances and counterexamples are powerful tests of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the peculiar and perpetual error of the human understanding to be more moved and excited by affirmatives than negatives... in establishing any true axiom the negative instance is the most powerful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek negative instances and counterexamples to test proposed axioms; prioritize falsifying evidence and use failures as decisive information when assessing generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dissection of nature and study of motions/laws of action over abstraction of forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is better to dissect than abstract nature... It is best to consider matter, its conformation, and the changes of that conformation, its own action, and the law of this action or motion; for forms are a mere fiction of the human mind...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus investigation on material structures, configurations, and dynamic laws rather than on metaphysical 'forms.' Analyze mechanisms and causal motions by experiment and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange analysis and synthesis: use both detailed particulars and general composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The contemplation of nature and of bodies in their individual form distracts and weakens the understanding; but the contemplation of nature... in their general composition and formation stupefies and relaxes it... These two species of contemplation must, therefore, be interchanged, and each employed in its turn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exclusive reliance on either minute particularism or sweeping generalities. Alternate between detailed study of differences and comparative study of resemblances to build a balanced, penetrating understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against human cognitive inclinations: immediacy, imagination, passion, and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: “The human understanding is most excited by that which strikes... imagination is immediately filled... the human understanding admits a tincture of the will and passions... man always believes more readily that which he prefers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedures (e.g., disciplined experiment, communal critique, replication) that mitigate biases from vivid instances, wishful thinking, and affective preferences. Do not let attractive or vivid examples dominate reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words can mislead; favor particular instances and ordered observation over verbal disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Words are generally formed in a popular sense... When a more acute understanding... is anxious to vary those lines, and to adapt them more accurately to nature, words oppose it... so that we must necessarily have recourse to particular instances, and their regular series and arrangement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering terminological disputes, resolve them by returning to concrete instances and ordered data rather than attempting to settle disputes by verbal definitions alone. Use definitions sparingly and anchor them in empirical series.
